question:
For greenfield metal deposits in north-east Russia that have no grid or road, which changes to power supply, construction method, access logistics or development order would cut full cost per unit delivered and the years from investment decision to first metal? The comparison is Kupol/Dvoinoye, Natalka, Baimskaya's 2020 plan, Red Dog and Meliadine. The answer must use only domestic or unrestricted equipment, and it must work through the period when Bilibino has closed and the floating units are not yet running (2026–2030).
Cases: Baimskaya copper-gold (Pevek/Nagleynyn route, Rosatom floating power units 2028–30); Chukotka and Magadan hard-rock and placer gold (Kupol, Natalka, Kolyma placers); Tomtor rare earths (Rosneft, pilot 2027, Anabar/Lena river access).
A good answer: (a) full cost per oz Au or per t Cu or rare-earth oxide delivered, including annualised external-infrastructure capex; (b) years from investment decision to first production, against Natalka (about 4–5 years, then 2 to full rate) and Baimskaya (end-2027 target, already slipped); (c) recovery, operating days per year, and life of tailings, dams and foundations in discontinuous or warm permafrost.
The binding constraint to attack: Firm power in the 2026–2030 gap (about 8 MW of winter spare in Chukotka), the capex of external road and port (Baimskaya rose from $5.5bn to $8bn, about $600m of it road and port), and short seasonal supply windows (winter roads, Pevek's 4–5-month navigation).
This is part 1 of 3 of a larger question (context, not instructions): Russia wants to develop and extract minerals and energy in its permafrost regions at the lowest full cost, in the shortest time from investment decision to first production, and with the highest effectiveness. Effectiveness means resource recovery, working time across the year, and how long infrastructure lasts on thawing ground. All three are measured per unit of product delivered to the buyer. T
notes:
The asker wants a professional, deeply sourced answer: hundreds of sources, numbers with units and years. Use official
Russian statistics and registers (Rosstat, Rosnedra, the Ministry of Natural Resources and its state reports on
mineral resources), company annual reports and presentations (Nornickel, Alrosa, Polyus, Rosneft, Novatek,
Gazprom Neft, Udokan Copper, Kaz Minerals for Baimskaya, Elga Coal), Russian-language technical literature (for
example the Melnikov Permafrost Institute of SB RAS and mining journals) as well as international sources. Proposals
must not depend on circumventing sanctions.
Assumptions in the question that may be wrong:

- The three measures can be traded off against each other, and one ordering of deposits is best.
- Thaw is the main cause of infrastructure failure, though engineering faults may be as important.
- All listed resources are in continuous permafrost, though some sit in discontinuous or no permafrost.
- The NSR is the main way to move product, but rail, river, or processing near the site may beat it.
- More output is the goal, though some listed projects may not be worth building at all.
Where deciding data may exist:

- Rosatom/NSR administration traffic statistics and ice-class fleet lists.
- Russian Ministry of Natural Resources (Rosnedra) reserves balance, the GKZ.
- Company reports from Nornickel, Polyus, Kinross-era Kupol, Novatek, Rosneft, Alrosa and Mechel/Elga.
- Permafrost temperature records: GTN-P and the Roshydromet/Earth Cryosphere Institute (Moscow) monitoring networks.
- Rostekhnadzor accident reports.
- Published capex and opex of the foreign benchmark mines (technical reports under Canadian NI 43-101 rules).
- Global Energy Monitor or IEA-style cost data for LNG.
What the parts share or compete for: - **Icebreakers:** the four project 22220 icebreakers in service, with Chukotka due in 2027, serve Part 2 (Ob Gulf, Kara Sea), Part 3 (year-round Dudinka) and Part 1 (Pevek in the eastern sector).
